signals.title: @theeyeofchange: THE SURVIELLANCE REPUBLIC (P4) In 2018, Google found itself under internal siege over Project Maven, a Pentagon program aimed at improving t
signals.content: THE SURVIELLANCE REPUBLIC (P4) In 2018, Google found itself under internal siege over Project Maven, a Pentagon program aimed at improving the military's AI-powered image-recognition software — technology intended to help analyze drone footage on the battlefield and, ultimately, assist in identifying and potentially striking targets. An open letter circulating internally and addressed to CEO Sundar Pichai collected over 3,100 signatures, and by some accounts the internal petition eventually grew to nearly 5,000 signatures, with dozens of employees resigning in protest. The letter itself argued plainly that "Google should not be in the business of war," framing the issue largely around reputational risk and brand damage. Beyond the letter's stated concerns, employees raised a range of other objections — some rooted in personal discomfort with contributing to military technology, others in broader unease about AI eventually playing a role in life-or-death targeting decisions on the battlefield. Google's leadership initially defended the contract — Google Cloud CEO Diane Greene told employees in an internal meeting that the technology would not be used to "operate or fly drones" or "launch weapons" — but the pressure campaign ultimately forced a partial retreat. Google announced it would not seek a follow-up contract once its existing Maven agreement expired in 2019, while still fulfilling the contract already in place. Peter Thiel was publicly critical of Google's decision at the time, framing it as effectively favoring business with China over the U.S. military — and Karp has echoed similar arguments in interviews since. Fittingly, Palantir stepped in and took over the Project Maven contract once Google backed away from it, reinforcing the company's reputation as a dependable partner for the Pentagon regardless of how Silicon Valley's political mood shifted. The relationship has only deepened since: Palantir won a $480 million, five-year contract in 2024 to expand the "Maven Smart System" to thousands of users across five combatant commands, and by 2025 the Pentagon had raised that contract ceiling to $1.3 billion through 2029, with more than 20,000 active users relying on the system. In 2020, Palantir relocated its headquarters from Palo Alto to Denver, Colorado — a symbolic break from the Silicon Valley culture that had generated so much of the friction over its work in the first place. Karp has used strikingly similar reasoning to defend both the Maven contract and Palantir's ICE work. In a Washington Post op-ed, he argued that Silicon Valley companies shouldn't be the ones setting government policy through their own contracting decisions — that even when he personally disagrees with certain policies of a democratically elected administration, tech companies shouldn't use their market power to override decisions made through the normal political process. He frames this as especially urgent in AI, given the risk of the U.S. falling behind geopolitical rivals. The trouble with this framing is that it assumes military AI development has to run through private contractors in the first place — companies that, as independent entities separate from the government, aren't obligated to accept any contract they find objectionable. One alternative would be for AI research on military applications to be done in-house by the government rather than outsourced. But that would undercut the entire business model companies like Palantir depend on, which puts Karp in an awkward bind: he wants to condemn Google for prioritizing its own interests over the country's, while simultaneously defending a system that depends on companies having exactly that freedom to choose. In the op-ed, Karp writes: "No company should have to work for the government. The challenge is when they want to accept lucrative law enforcement or military contracts with one hand while stiff-arming the government with the other." This is where the argument runs into trouble. Google wasn't taking government money while withholding its product — it simply declined to renew a contract once its existing obligations were fulfilled. Karp's framing implies Google was still collecting payment while refusing delivery, which isn't what happened. If his real position is that a company which has taken government contracts in the past is obligated to keep taking them going forward, that amounts to arguing that any company that has ever worked with the military must accept any future military contract it's offered — a standard that neither reflects how contracting works nor one Palantir itself would likely want applied to its own business. Source: The Billionaire CEO Who Controls Your Data

signals.title: An Agentic Approach for Active Data Collection, Travel Behavior Modeling, and Weather-Sensitive Demand Prediction
signals.content: Travel behavior research increasingly combines digital data collection with predictive modeling, yet these stages are often developed and evaluated separately. This study proposes a three-agent workflow integrating conversational data collection, structured data processing, and behavioral prediction. A chatbot-administered, image-augmented stated-preference survey collected mode choices from student commuters across five predefined weather scenarios, yielding 454 respondent-scenario observations. Weather-related associations were analyzed using a multinomial logit model, while logistic regression and random forest provided machine-learning benchmarks. Nine locally deployed large language models (LLMs), ranging from 2 to 35 billion parameters, were evaluated across four zero-shot prompt-and-context conditions and extended through persona, few-shot, and vision-based configurations. Random forest achieved 69.6% five-class accuracy, while the best text-only zero-shot LLM reached 69.9% without task-specific fitting. Habitual travel information produced the most consistent gains, Expert framing generally outperformed Role-Play, and persona information was most useful when habitual travel information was unavailable. Few-shot prompting improved prediction for several models, with gains stabilizing after a small number of examples. Using the same weather images shown to respondents, the best vision-based configuration reached 71.5% five-class accuracy, indicating that visual context may provide additional predictive information for selected models. Overall, the study shows how conversational surveys, structured data processing, conventional behavioral modeling, machine learning, and multimodal LLM prediction can be coordinated within an auditable multi-agent workflow.

signals.title: Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
signals.content: Large language model (LLM) agents can induce skills from completed tasks and reuse them later to grow more capable with experience. In practice, induced skills may transfer unreliably and can even harm the agent that retrieves them. When agent-induced skills transfer reliably across tasks remains an open question. We conduct a comprehensive and controlled study of how the way skills are induced shapes their transfer across tasks. Specifically, we compare task-level with subtask-level skill induction and text with code skill formats, the two axes along which existing methods differ. Task-level skills mostly reduce the agent's performance below its no-memory baseline while subtask-level skills raise it above on average, and text skills transfer better than code skills. To further understand our findings, we examine two complementary properties of the induced skills: specificity, which measures how closely a skill matches real tasks, and abstractness, which measures how evenly its relevance spreads across tasks. Neither property alone predicts task success, but their combined effect does, which we propose as a skill utility score. The score correlates consistently with task success when skills are transferred, and subtask-level and text skills score higher. Computing skill utility only needs the skills and task descriptions but not any task execution, so our score serves as a practical diagnostic of a skill memory before any new task runs.

The same advanced chips and models that drive American innovation can, in the wrong hands, accelerate cyberattacks, autonomous weapons, and the surveillance regimes of authoritarian rivals. Protecting that advantage is inseparable from using it responsibly. Maintaining American leadership means keeping our most advanced technology out of adversaries’ hands: enforcing export controls, closing the loopholes that let restricted chips slip through, and securing supply chains against theft and espionage. signals.content: NEW SATELLITE IMAGERY — SYRIA High-resolution Airbus satellite imagery published by Soar Atlas provides a clearer look at the damage caused by Israeli airstrikes on Abu al-Duhur Military Airbase in northwestern Syria. Coordinates: 35.734°N, 37.102°E The strikes were carried out on August 18, with Syrian state media reporting eight separate Israeli attacks targeting the runway and storage facilities at the base. No casualties were reported. The imagery shows visible damage along the airfield infrastructure, consistent with reports that the runway was one of the primary targets. Abu al-Duhur is located roughly 70 km from the Turkish border and has recently gained renewed strategic importance. Syrian officials say the facility was being rehabilitated for use by the Syrian Air Force. Turkish military officers had also visited the base as part of training and military cooperation between Ankara and Damascus. Syria denies that Turkey planned to establish a permanent military base or deploy forces there. Israel, however, said it acted after concerns that a Turkish military presence at Abu al-Duhur could threaten Israeli security and alter the regional security status quo. The strike has increased tensions between Israel and Turkey, while U.S. envoy Tom Barrack described the attack as an “unnecessary escalation.” Location: Abu al-Duhur Military Airbase, Syria 35.734°N, 37.102°E

signals.title: MidTool: Mid-training Data Synthesis for Agentic Tool Use
signals.content: Mid-training is increasingly recognized as a critical stage for shaping the capabilities of large language models. Recent work has shown that targeted mid-training can strengthen reasoning-intensive abilities such as math and science, and can also improve agentic capabilities in software-engineering settings. In this work, we study the parallel but less explored agentic capability: general tool use. We present MidTool, an open corpus construction pipeline for agentic tool-use mid-training that combines large-scale web, PDF, and code data with synthesized supervision from real-world tool APIs, MCP skills, and document-grounded workflows. MidTool is designed to teach models how to recognize tool affordances, ground arguments from context, compose tool call workflow, and recover from incomplete information. We mid-train Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base on MidTool-Mix, and then apply follow-up post-training with both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Compared with baselines, MidTool-Mix consistently improves downstream performance under both SFT and RL on BFCL, tau2-Bench, and MCP Universe. These results suggest that general tool use, like other important LLM capabilities, benefits from dedicated mid-training rather than being left entirely to post-training.
